hardware: The physical machine itself: the CPU, memory and the circuits that check permissions. Software asks; hardware enforces.
bit: A single 0 or 1. A permission like writable is stored as one bit inside a larger number.
null pointer: A pointer to address 0. Most systems protect page 0 so that using it by mistake crashes loudly. Out of scope here.
swapping: Moving memory pages out to disk when RAM is full, and back later. Not part of this project.
copy-on-write: A trick where parent and child share pages after fork and only copy a page when one of them writes it. xv6 here copies up front instead.
thread: An independent flow of execution inside one process that shares its memory. xv6 here has none, which makes the check-then-write safe.
memory: The numbered storage a running program reads and writes. The hardware divides it into pages.
mprotect: A system call that makes pages read-only. Say it as "em-protect". Its partner munprotect undoes it.
page: A fixed block of memory, 4096 bytes on x86. Permissions are set per page, never per byte.
CPU: The processor that runs instructions. It checks the permission bits on every single memory access.
process: A running program with its own private memory. Killing one process does not affect another.
fork: A system call that creates a child process: a copy of the parent with its own copy of every page.
kernel: The privileged core of the operating system. It runs with more rights than ordinary programs and handles system calls.
system call: A numbered request from a program to the kernel, like open, read or mprotect. The only door into the kernel.
dispatch table: An array indexed by system call number whose slots hold the handler functions. Slot 22 holds sys_mprotect.
handler: The function that deals with one request. Here, sys_mprotect is the handler for system call 22.
page table: A data structure in memory that maps virtual pages to physical pages and holds their permission bits.
interrupt: A signal that makes the CPU stop what it is doing and jump into the kernel. A system call uses a software interrupt (int).
stack: A program's scratch space for function arguments and local variables. System call arguments are read from it.
EAX: A general-purpose CPU register. By convention the call number goes in on the way in, and the result comes back in it.
macro: A named template the compiler expands before compiling. #define lines in C, and SYSCALL in usys.S, are macros.
virtual address: The address a program uses. The CPU translates it to a real physical address through the page table.
physical address: The real location in RAM. Programs never see it; the page table hides it.
PTE: Page table entry: a 32-bit value holding a physical page number and permission flags such as present, writable and user.
trap: A transfer of control into the kernel caused by an event: a system call, a fault, or an interrupt. Trap 14 is a page fault.
page fault: The CPU's complaint when an access is not allowed, for example writing a read-only page. xv6 kills the process that caused it.
CR2: A CPU register that holds the address that caused the most recent page fault. rcr2() reads it.
CR3: A CPU register holding the physical address of the current page directory. Writing it also flushes the TLB.
int: C's signed whole number. A negative page count is possible, which is why the helper rejects counts of 0 or less.
overflow: When arithmetic produces a number too big for its size and wraps around. In 32 bits, 2^32 wraps to 0.
guard page: An unmapped-for-users page placed below the stack so that running off the stack faults. Its user bit is cleared, so our helper refuses it.
TLB: Translation lookaside buffer: a small CPU cache of recent address translations, including their permissions. It can go stale.
cache: A fast copy of something slow to read. When the original changes, the copy must be refreshed or discarded.
loop: Code that repeats. The helper loops over every page twice: once to check, once to change.
register: A tiny, very fast storage slot inside the CPU. CR3 and EAX are registers.
buffer: A block of memory used to hold data being moved, such as the array read() fills in.
CR0.WP: A CPU switch (write-protect). When set, even kernel code obeys read-only pages. xv6 sets it.
panic: xv6's response to an unrecoverable kernel bug: print a message and halt the whole machine.
lock: A mechanism that lets only one CPU or thread use something at a time. Needed if two things could change a page between a check and a write.
pipe: A one-way channel between processes. Bytes written at one end can be read at the other; end-of-file arrives when all writers are gone.
mutation testing: Deliberately breaking the code to check that your tests notice. A test that never fails proves nothing.
CI: Continuous integration: a service (GitHub Actions here) that builds and tests the project automatically on every push.
guest: The xv6 system running inside QEMU. It is separate from your real computer.
scratch copy: A throwaway copy of the project used for experiments, so the real repository stays untouched.
wrapper: A thin function that adds nothing but a different way to call another function.
